title: Tenali Raman Tale 80

full_text:
A wealthy, absent-minded merchant named Narahari was taking a sacred bath in the Tungabhadra River before sunrise. Having a valuable gold ring set with a large sapphire, he was afraid it might slip off in the deep water.
He walked onto the wide, sandy riverbank, dug a small hole, placed his sapphire ring inside, and covered it with sand.
To remember the spot, he looked up at the sky and saw a fluffy, white morning cloud shaped like a sleeping elephant directly above the hole!
'Excellent!' thought Narahari. 'My ring is buried directly beneath the sleeping elephant cloud!'

After bathing for an hour, Narahari returned to the sand to retrieve his ring.
He looked up: the wind had blown the clouds across the sky!
The sleeping elephant cloud was now three miles away, hovering over the dense forest!
Narahari ran frantically across the forest, digging under every tree, crying that someone had stolen his cloud and his ring!

The weeping merchant came to Tenali Raman.
Tenali listened to his absurd story, chuckled, and said:
'Narahari, he who ties his memory to drifting clouds will spend his life digging in the wind!
Come, let us find thy ring.'

Tenali did not look at the sky.
He asked Narahari: 'When thou didst bury the ring, what did thy feet feel under the sand?'
Narahari remembered: 'My left heel stepped on a large, flat, cold stone slab near the water's edge.'
'And which way was thy shadow falling?'
'The sun was just rising behind the eastern temple spire; my shadow fell straight toward the river.'

Tenali walked to the riverbank, located the flat stone slab, calculated the angle of the sunrise shadow from the temple spire, and marked a circle in the sand thirty paces from the water.
Tenali took a wooden spade, dug two feet into the sand—and out came the sapphire gold ring!

Narahari wept with joy, embracing Tenali:
'Tenali, thou hast recovered my fortune!'
Tenali smiled warmly:
'Remember, Narahari: clouds change their shape and blow away with every breeze, but the temple spire and the stone slab stand firm.
Never anchor thy trust, thy promises, or thy treasures to shifting illusions; anchor them to steadfast truth.'
moral: Fixing reference marks upon shifting, moving objects guarantees failure; anchor thy memory to the eternal.
